text: So far we've only read data. Now we write it — creating new records, changing existing ones, and removing records, each with its own distinct pattern, and each pattern looks a little different from the query pattern you already know.

To insert a new record, call initialize first — that sets up a blank in-memory record with the table's default values applied, and it does not touch the database. Then set fields with setValue or dot notation, both are valid for writing. Insert is the call that actually saves the row, and it returns the new record's sys_id as a string, or null if the insert failed. Capturing that return value matters whenever you need to reference the new record right after creating it.

Updating is always find, change, save. Query and next locate the existing record first — notice there's no initialize call here at all, because initialize is only for building a brand-new blank record. Once next returns true, you're working with an already-populated record, so you just set the fields you want to change and call update to save them.

deleteRecord removes exactly one record — the one the cursor is currently positioned on. You have to call next first to position it there, exactly like reading or updating a single record. Call it without first finding a record, and there's simply nothing positioned to delete.

deleteMultiple works completely differently. It deletes every record matching the current query in one operation, with no while-next loop required at all. That makes it efficient for bulk cleanup, but also dangerous — a query that's broader than you intended deletes more than you intended, with no per-row confirmation. Always verify the addQuery conditions first, ideally by running the same query with a normal loop and logging what it matches before calling deleteMultiple for real.

Insert needs initialize; update needs query and next first; deleteRecord removes one row at a time, deleteMultiple removes them all at once with no loop. Keep those four patterns distinct in your head and you'll reach for the right one every time. Next lesson: encoded queries and the other addQuery variants — operators, null checks, OR conditions, and sorting.
